title: Code Generation Scores Don’t Predict Software That Works
dek: Benchmarks can reveal whether a model solves a bounded coding task, but they say much less about whether it will preserve requirements, integrate with a framework, and survive real workflows. Production evaluation must measure the whole repair-and-verification loop.
by: Draft for team review · written by a language model from engineers' public reports · checked in code
lead: Coding scores are useful for comparing performance on a defined task, but they do not establish that a model will build dependable software in a real repository. Evaluate models on representative changes, exact constraints, integration and regression tests, human repair effort, and total workflow cost—not token price or a benchmark rank alone.
decisions: Choose evaluations that resemble your repository and acceptance criteria.
Measure requirement fidelity, regressions, integration, and repair effort separately.
Compare total verified-outcome cost, not token prices or rankings alone.
Retest when models, prompts, tools, or repository workflows change.
body: A code-generation score is a result under a particular task definition, harness, and success criterion. It may tell an engineering team whether a model can produce an answer that passes the harness. It does not, by itself, tell the team whether the model can interpret an incomplete product brief, select the right abstractions, integrate with a particular framework, preserve existing behavior, or deliver a usable application. Those are related capabilities, but they are not interchangeable. The central evaluation mistake is to treat a narrow measure of task completion as a general forecast of software delivery.

Benchmarks built around a known expected answer or a clear test oracle measure something valuable: whether the system can move from a provided task description to a verifiable state. That is a real production advantage when the environment provides reliable tests and the task can be decomposed into observable outcomes. A practitioner highlights this condition with «If you can build a verification system and give proper direction». The qualification matters. A benchmark with a clean oracle may reward code that conforms to a test while leaving untested requirements, framework conventions, and operational failure modes outside the score. The result is not meaningless; it is narrower than broad claims about coding ability imply.
If you can build a verification system and give proper direction

A second weakness is that leaderboard comparisons often compress a multidimensional process into one ordering. An evaluation can rank a model for task success while omitting how many attempts it took, how much context or output it consumed, whether it introduced unnecessary complexity, and how much supervision was needed. One practitioner cautions, «you should look at how much you pay for the entire process». That is a better unit of comparison for production: not token price or isolated pass rate, but the cost of obtaining a verified change, including retries, review, debugging, and integration. Scores should be reported with their task conditions and process costs, rather than presented as a universal verdict.

body.text: What the score misses in real repositories

body: A repository is not a collection of independent coding puzzles. A requested feature crosses data models, user interface, authentication, persistence, framework conventions, deployment dependencies, and older behavior. A model can generate attractive, plausible forms while omitting specified functions or binding them incorrectly to existing objects. In one business-software build, the first implementation had functional-looking screens but missed certificate generation, statistics, and an externally accessible survey; later, invoice and project actions still failed, and refreshing a particular order broke its view. The relevant distinction is between producing code and completing the behavior users depend on.

Integration errors expose why local success is an incomplete measure. A generated component may be syntactically valid and still conflict with the host application’s styling, routing, model relationships, or expectations about state after a page reload. The same build encountered stylesheet conflicts and confusion between custom training orders and a built-in Orders application. These are not evidence that every model will fail in the same way, nor do they establish one general cause. They demonstrate that framework familiarity and system boundaries are part of the workload, and that a benchmark which starts from a self-contained function will not necessarily measure them.
It ignored them and imagined totally another values

Requirement fidelity deserves its own measure rather than being inferred from broad coding competence. A model that substitutes invented configuration values, skips a condition, or adds elaborate machinery may produce code that looks coherent while violating the brief. A Terraform user says, «It ignored them and imagined totally another values». That is a single reported outcome, not a comparative benchmark result, but it identifies a failure category evaluations should explicitly probe: does the model preserve user-specified constants and constraints, and does it surface ambiguity instead of silently resolving it? A useful score needs separate accounting for omitted requirements, altered values, unsupported assumptions, regressions, and cosmetic defects. Otherwise, a passing result can conceal the exact mistakes that are costly to catch in review.

body.text: Why practitioner experience diverges from rankings

body: A benchmark result and a day-to-day workflow can both be honestly reported and still disagree. Their tasks differ, their context differs, and their definition of success differs. Benchmarks often constrain the request and provide a known evaluation path; production work includes local conventions, dependency behavior, incomplete specifications, and feedback from tests or users. An engineer may experience a model as more capable because it follows instructions clearly in a familiar stack, while an aggregate score rewards performance on a different task mix. Neither observation alone establishes a universal model ordering.

Model version changes also make a score a time- and setup-specific observation, not a permanent property. Reports of regressions and improvements in particular workflows do not establish why a change occurred. One user reports, «Within minutes, it communicates clearly :O It builds properly» after returning to an earlier model. Another says a newer model ignored values in a Terraform request while an earlier model produced a working first attempt. These reports are useful signals for designing controlled tests, not proof that the earlier model is generally superior. Differences in prompts, repository state, tools, settings, or task selection can all confound a direct comparison; where the cause is not established, it should remain explicitly unknown.
Within minutes, it communicates clearly :O It builds properly

Task decomposition can change the result more than a model label suggests. In a real feature build, one model planned the work, another executed it, and a human tested the application and supplied further detail. The eventual completion in a person-day is therefore a system outcome involving foundation software, specification quality, iterative prompting, and human verification—not a standalone model score. Conversely, a pipeline that uses a narrow deterministic check before invoking a model can avoid unnecessary generations and reduce failure exposure. A game implementation, for example, used a pixel-similarity check to award a known item when the drawing was close enough to a template, reserving image classification for cases that needed it. This is a design lesson for evaluation: measure the architecture around generation, not just the generator.

Build an evaluation from the changes your team actually ships. Select representative tasks from real repositories: constrained configuration edits, bug fixes with regressions, framework-specific features, and changes that cross a UI and persistence boundary. Preserve the relevant repository context and tooling, and define acceptance conditions before running models. Include both tasks with crisp automated oracles and tasks whose requirements require human review. A test suite should check not only whether the expected behavior appears, but whether existing behavior remains intact and whether constraints in the prompt are followed exactly.

Run comparable attempts under controlled conditions, then record more than pass or fail. Track the fraction of requirements satisfied, defects introduced, test failures, retries, human intervention, elapsed work, and the model’s input and output consumption. Inspect the diff for unnecessary complexity and verify behavior through the same build, test, and deployment steps used in normal engineering. Keep task-specific results visible rather than collapsing them prematurely into a single average: an overall score can hide that a model is excellent at isolated edits but unreliable at framework integration. Repeat after model or workflow changes, since a previous result should not be assumed to transfer to a new version or prompt strategy.
you should look at how much you pay for the entire process

Registry list prices show that Claude Opus 5 is priced at $5.00 input and $25.00 output per million tokens, while Kimi K2.6 is $0.65 input and $3.41 output per million tokens; those prices alone do not establish which costs less to deliver a correct change. A practitioner explicitly warns that a lower-priced model may require more tokens and more management, concluding, «you should look at how much you pay for the entire process». Measure actual usage alongside the repair loop, and include the cost of human review and failed attempts. Cached-input prices and advertised context windows are operational inputs, not evidence of coding quality or effective context use.

The right conclusion from a benchmark is consequently modest but useful: under the stated conditions, a model achieved a measured result. For an architecture decision, ask whether those conditions resemble your codebase, whether the evaluation verifies the behavior you need, and whether the complete workflow remains economical and controllable. Make failure modes visible, preserve an option to route a task to a different model or a human, and validate changes against the production acceptance criteria. Code generation is not a single ability captured by one ranking. It is a chain from requirements through edits to verified behavior, and an evaluation earns trust only when it measures that chain closely enough to support the decision being made.
